description:
Inspects the TLS certificate a host actually serves: when it expires, who issued it,
whether the chain verifies, which hostnames it covers, and which TLS version was
negotiated.

Use it to answer "when does this certificate need renewing?", "why does the browser warn
about this site?" or "does the certificate cover www as well as the bare domain?" — the
last being one of the most common real-world misconfigurations, along with a missing
intermediate certificate, which is reported as UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE.

When the host is the bare domain or its www, and the certificate does not cover the other
one while that one resolves, a second handshake is made with it: many sites serve www from a
separate certificate, so only what the other name actually serves decides the finding.
www_not_covered / apex_not_covered mean what it serves is not valid for it;
www_https_failed / apex_https_failed mean no secure connection could be made there;
*_coverage_unjudged means it could not be established either way. A deeper host's
certificate is not judged on the bare domain or www — check those by name.

Do not use it for domain registration expiry, which is a different date entirely — that is
domain_check. It connects to the host but does not request a page; use uptime_check for that.

Certificates that are expired, self-signed or untrusted are inspected and reported rather
than refused. Revocation is checked over OCSP, preferring the response a server staples to
the handshake and otherwise asking the issuing authority directly; the answer is only
believed once its signature verifies against that authority and while it is current, and a
staple that fails either is not the end of it: the authority is asked anyway. Many healthy
certificates cannot be checked at all, because since 2025 the two largest issuers publish no OCSP
responder and distribute revocation by CRL instead — that is reported as an unavailable
reason rather than as a problem with the site, and produces no finding. Certificate
revocation lists are not downloaded.

For a Let's Encrypt certificate it also reads the renewal window the authority publishes
(RFC 9773). Still serving a certificate after that window closed is reported as
cert_renewal_overdue: the renewal has probably stopped, even with weeks left to run. Other
issuers are not asked, which is reported as a reason and produces no finding. It also
compares the domain's CAA records with the certificate's issuer: a certificate keeps working
when CAA stops allowing its issuer, and the next renewal then fails (caa_excludes_issuer).

When a certificate is called out depends on how long it lives: a 90-day certificate is a
warning inside 14 days and critical inside seven, a 45-day one inside 7 and 4, a 6-day one
inside 1 and on its last day, and a longer one warns at most 30 days ahead. An ACME client
renews a 90-day certificate with 30 days left, so 28 remaining is a healthy site in the
middle of a normal renewal, not a problem. Returns findings ordered by urgency, worst first.

domain.description: The host whose certificate should be inspected, e.g. "example.com" — no scheme, no trailing slash. A full URL is also accepted and reduced to its hostname. The certificate is read for exactly this host, so "www.example.com" and "example.com" are different checks. A bare public suffix such as "co.uk" is refused.

port.description: TCP port to connect to, as an integer, e.g. 8443. Defaults to 443. Use 8443, 993 and so on for other services when running locally; a hosted (HTTP) instance refuses every port but 443.

name: ssl_check

caaAllowsThisIssuer.description: Whether the domain's CAA records allow the authority that issued this certificate to issue its replacement. Null when nothing can be said: no record restricts issuance, the issuer is not one this tool has identifiers for, the DNS lookup or its CAA query failed, or the host is neither the apex nor www. False is `caa_excludes_issuer`.

chain.description: The certificate chain and whether it verified.

error.description: Why it did not verify, e.g. "CERT_HAS_EXPIRED", "UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE" (a missing intermediate). Only one reason is reported even when several things are wrong.

issuers.description: Issuer common names, from the leaf upwards.

length.description: Certificates in the chain, including the trust-store root when verified.

revocationChecked.description: Whether a signed answer from the issuing authority established the revocation status. False is common and usually harmless: since 2025 the two largest issuers publish no OCSP responder at all. See `revocation` for what was established and why.

valid.description: Whether the chain verified against the system trust store.

checkedAt.description: When the check ran, ISO 8601 in UTC.

coverage.description: Which hostnames this certificate is valid for.

coversApex.description: Whether the certificate covers the registrable domain itself.

coversRequestedHost.description: Whether the certificate is valid for the host asked about.

coversWww.description: Whether the certificate covers "www." plus the registrable domain.

matchedVia.description: Which SAN entry matched, e.g. "*.example.com". Null when nothing matched.

host.description: The sibling that was contacted, e.g. "www.example.com" or "example.com".

matchedVia.description: Which SAN entry of the sibling's own certificate matched, when one did.

outcome.description: "valid" means the sibling serves its own certificate and browsers accept it there, so nothing is wrong; "invalid" means what it serves does not cover it or does not verify; "failed" means no secure connection could be made to it at all; "unjudged" means it could not be established either way, e.g. a timeout.

problem.description: What is wrong, or why nothing was established. Null when valid.

sibling.description: What the other one of the apex and its www serves itself. Only checked when the host asked about is one of the two, this certificate does not cover the other, and the other resolves: a site may serve www and the apex from separate certificates, and only a handshake with the sibling says whether visitors there see a warning. Null when not checked.

subjectAltName.description: The raw subjectAltName extension, for display.

wwwResolves.description: Whether "www." resolves at all. Missing www coverage only matters when it does. Null when DNS could not be consulted, in which case that coverage was not judged.

daysUntilExpiry.description: Whole days until the certificate expires, negative if already expired. Floored, so a certificate expiring in a few hours reads as 0.

expiresAt.description: When the certificate expires, ISO 8601 UTC.

items.description: One actionable observation about the target.

code.description: Stable identifier for this kind of observation, e.g. "cert_expires_soon".

message.description: One sentence explaining the observation in plain words.

severity.description: How much attention this needs. "critical" means act now; "warning" means act this month; "unknown" means the check could not establish the fact, which is not the same as it being fine.

host.description: The host that was contacted, in ASCII (punycode) form.

issuedAt.description: Start of the certificate validity, ISO 8601 UTC.

issuer.description: Issuer common name, e.g. "R11" or "GTS CA 1P5".

lifetimeDays.description: Whole days from issue to expiry, which sets when this certificate is called out. `null` when the dates cannot be read.

renewalInfo.description: When the issuing authority wants this certificate renewed.

checked.description: Whether the issuing authority published a renewal window for this certificate (ACME Renewal Information, RFC 9773). False is common and says nothing about the site: only Let's Encrypt is asked.

explanationUrl.description: Where the authority explains a window it moved, when it says.

unavailableReason.description: Why this was not checked. `null` when it was.

windowEnd.description: When that window closes, ISO 8601 UTC. Still being served after this is `cert_renewal_overdue`.

windowStart.description: When the authority wants renewal attempted from, ISO 8601 UTC.

revocation.description: Whether the certificate has been revoked, and how confidently that was established.

checked.description: Whether a current, signed answer from the issuing authority was obtained and verified. The one field to branch on: `status` can be set while this is false, which means an answer arrived but could not be traced to the authority that issued the certificate, or was out of date.

nextUpdate.description: When a fresher answer will be published, ISO 8601 UTC. Typically about a week out, because responders pre-sign their answers.

producedAt.description: When the responder produced this answer, ISO 8601 UTC.

reason.description: Why it was revoked, e.g. "keyCompromise", "superseded", "cessationOfOperation". Null when the responder did not state one.

responder.description: The OCSP responder that was contacted, e.g. "http://ocsp.digicert.com". Set even when the query failed, so a responder that would not answer is distinguishable from a certificate that names none.

revokedAt.description: When the certificate was revoked, ISO 8601 UTC. Null unless revoked.

signatureVerified.description: Whether the answer's signature verified against the issuing certificate authority. An OCSP response travels over plain HTTP by design; the signature, not the transport, is what makes it evidence.

source.description: Where the answer came from. "stapled" means the server included it in the handshake, which costs no request at all; "responder" means the issuing authority was asked directly.

status.description: What the responder said. "good" means not revoked; "revoked" means it was withdrawn before its expiry date and browsers that check will refuse the site; "unknown" means the authority does not recognise the serial number. Null when no answer was obtained.

unavailableReason.description: Why nothing was established, e.g. "the certificate names no OCSP responder, so its issuer distributes revocation by certificate revocation list only". Null when the status was established.

severity.description: How much attention this needs. "critical" means act now; "warning" means act this month; "unknown" means the check could not establish the fact, which is not the same as it being fine.

alpn.description: Negotiated ALPN protocol, e.g. "h2". Null when none was agreed.

title: SSL certificate
